subject: physics_2
question_text: Define half life period and decay constant for a radioactive substance. Deduce the relation between them.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: N = N₀e⁻λt with N = N₀/2 at t = T gives e^λT = 2, so λT = logₑ2 = 0.6931 and T = 0.693/λ. Cross-check with the mean life τ = 1/λ: T = 0.693τ, the standard result. The book's working is followed line for line.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Half life period
steps.mark_note: Time for half the nuclei to disintegrate
lines: Half life period (T): the time taken for the
number of radioactive nuclei in a sample to
fall to half its original number is called the
steps.margin_note: First mark. "Half of the ORIGINAL number" — not half of what is left at any moment.
steps.why: The definition is written in terms of a fraction, not a fixed number of nuclei, which is why the half life is the same whatever the size of the sample.
common_mistakes: Saying the time for the whole sample to decay. That time is never reached.
Saying half life depends on the amount taken. It does not.

recall.must_convey: That the half life period is the time in which the number of radioactive nuclei falls to half of its original number.
accept: time to reduce to half of the original number
half of the nuclei disintegrate in that time
reject: ratio of the rate of decay to the number present

steps.memory_tip: Half life is set by the nucleus alone; the size of the sample does not enter.

steps.label: Decay constant
lines: Decay constant (λ): the ratio of the rate of
radioactive decay to the number of nuclei
It is a constant for a given substance, with
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The defining ratio and the unit s⁻¹.
steps.why: λ is the fraction of the nuclei present that decay in one second, so it is a property of the nucleus and does not change as the sample runs down.
common_mistakes: Writing λ = dN/dt without dividing by N. That is the activity, not λ.

recall.must_convey: That the decay constant is the ratio of the rate of decay to the number of nuclei present, with unit per second.
accept: rate of decay divided by the number present
minus dN by dt over N

steps.memory_tip: λ is a fraction per second; T is a time. They must be reciprocally related.

steps.label: Substitute in the decay law
steps.mark_note: Put N = N₀/2 at t = T
lines: By the definition of half life, at t = T the
number left is N = N₀/2. So
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The substitution N = N₀/2 at t = T is the whole step.
steps.why: N₀ cancels on both sides, which is the algebraic reason the half life does not depend on how much material was taken.
common_mistakes: Substituting N = N₀/2 at t = 0. The halving happens at t = T.

recall.must_convey: That putting N = N₀/2 at t = T into N = N₀e^(−λt) gives e^(λT) = 2.
accept: put N equals N nought by two at t equals T
e to the power lambda T equals two
reject: T equals zero point six nine three by lambda

steps.memory_tip: Half of the sample left is the ONLY extra fact the derivation needs.

steps.label: The relation
lines: So the half life period and the decay constant
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The boxed relation T = 0.693/λ.
steps.why: logₑ2 = 0.693 is the only number in the result, so a large λ (fast decay) always goes with a short half life.
common_mistakes: Writing T = 0.693λ. The λ is in the denominator.

recall.must_convey: That taking logarithms gives lambda T equal to log of 2, so T equals 0.693 divided by lambda.
accept: T equals zero point six nine three by lambda
reject: N equals N nought e to the minus lambda t

steps.memory_tip: One number to remember: 0.693, always over λ.

insider_note: Both definitions must be written before the derivation; a derivation with no definitions loses half the marks even when the algebra is right.
